description: We are She’ar Force, a team of two female mechanical engineering students passionate about space exploration and innovation. With skills in engineering analysis, mathematical modeling, Python, and MATLAB, we aim to develop creative, practical, and scientifically grounded solutions. Through NASA Space Apps, we hope to combine our technical knowledge and creativity to tackle real-world space challenges.
summary: At the lunar south pole, the Sun never rises more than about 7° above the horizon, so surrounding ridges can easily block both sunlight and the view of Earth. She’ar Force asks a simple question for three Artemis III sample sites: when are the Sun and Earth both visible at once? We combined hourly Sun and Earth directions from NASA/JPL Horizons with terrain skylines built from NASA LOLA south-polar elevation models. Together they cover 721 hours, from 14 November to 14 December 2026. The results differ sharply from site to site. At Mons Mouton (MM-01), both bodies are above the skyline in 53.8% of hours. At Mons Mouton Plateau (MMP-02), the figure is 26.8%, in a single window. At Nobile Rim 1 (NR-03), it is 0%, a result we flag for independent verification. Our cinematic website lets users replay the month from the surface and explore coordinates, and it reports clearly when there isn’t enough data. This is a line-of-sight research prototype. It does not assess power, communications or landing safety.
details:
Our project uses NASA’s open Earth observation data to turn complex scientific information into a simple, interactive platform that anyone can use. Users choose a location or topic of interest, and the system processes the related satellite data to show clear visualizations, trends and easy-to-understand insights. The main benefit is that it makes valuable space data accessible to students, local communities and decision-makers who don’t have technical expertise. Our intended impact is to raise awareness of environmental changes and help people make faster, better-informed decisions for a more sustainable future.

We developed the project with Python for data processing and JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the user interface, and used GitHub for teamwork and version control. It is creative because it combines different NASA datasets in one place and presents them in a visual, user-friendly way, so raw data becomes something people can actually act on. During development, our team considered accessibility, data accuracy, ease of use, low cost through free and open-source tools, and the possibility of expanding the platform to new regions and datasets in the future.
